name: Andronicus (kinsman of Paul)
title: Early apostle and fellow prisoner with Paul
summary: Andronicus is mentioned in Romans 16:7 as a highly respected figure in the early Christian movement. He was of Jewish origin and described by Paul as both a relative and fellow prisoner, testifying to shared suffering for the sake of the gospel. Together with Junia, he was regarded as outstanding among the apostles – an expression that in Christian tradition has been understood to mean they held apostolic recognition, although some scholars interpret it differently. Notably, both had come to faith in Christ before Paul, placing them among the very first Christians. Their relationship to each other – whether spouses, siblings, or coworkers – is not further specified in the text, but Christian tradition has often assumed they were a married couple.

keyEvents.title: Greeting from Paul
keyEvents.description: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia in his letter to the church in Rome, speaking of them with great respect and warmth, which suggests a close and long-standing relationship between them.

keyEvents.title: Identified as Paul's kinsman and fellow prisoner
keyEvents.description: Paul calls Andronicus his kinsman (Greek: syngenēs) and fellow prisoner (Greek: synaichmalōtos). The first term indicates Jewish origin and possibly kinship, while the second shows that Andronicus at some unknown time shared imprisonment with Paul for the sake of the gospel.

keyEvents.title: Prominent among the apostles
keyEvents.description: Paul describes Andronicus and Junia as prominent among the apostles (Greek: episēmoi en tois apostolois). This has traditionally been understood to mean that they themselves were counted as apostles with a significant role in the early church, although some scholars interpret it as meaning they were well regarded by the apostles.

keyEvents.title: Early conversion to Christ
keyEvents.description: Andronicus and Junia had come to faith in Christ before Paul, which places their conversion in the very earliest period of the Christian movement, possibly as early as around AD 30–33, perhaps in connection with the first Pentecost in Jerusalem.

versions.summary: Andronicus was a Jewish Christian whom Paul refers to as his relative and fellow prisoner. He and Junia were highly regarded among the apostles and had come to faith in Christ before Paul himself.
versions.title: Apostle Before Paul
versions.reason: [minor] The title "Apostle Before Paul" may give the impression that he held a formal rank as an apostle prior to Paul, but what Paul writes is that he came to faith before him and was prominent among the apostles. A slightly more nuanced title might be better.; [minor] It is a widespread interpretation that Andronicus and Junia were spouses, but this is not explicitly confirmed in the biblical text. Romans 16:7 mentions them together but does not state they were married. This should be noted as an interpretation, even though it is the most common one.; [major] All keyEvents use 'verse' (singular) instead of 'verses' (plural as an array) in their scripture references. The schema requires 'verses' as an array of integers.; [minor] The role "servant" is generic. "Missionary" or "evangelist" may be more appropriate given that he was a fellow prisoner with Paul and prominent among the apostles, which suggests active missionary work.; [major] Footnotes are missing. This profile has several interesting theological, linguistic, and historical aspects that should be covered, for example, the debate over "episēmoi en tois apostolois" (prominent among the apostles versus well known by the apostles), and the debate over Junia/Junias (woman/man).

footnotes.text: The Greek expression 'episēmoi en tois apostolois' in Romans 16:7 has been the subject of considerable debate. It can be translated either as 'prominent among the apostles' (inclusive interpretation, meaning they themselves were apostles) or 'well regarded by the apostles' (exclusive interpretation). Most early church fathers, including John Chrysostom, interpreted it to mean that Andronicus and Junia were prominent apostles.

The name Andronicus (Greek: Ἀνδρόνικος) means 'male victory' or 'victor'. It was a common Greek name in the Hellenistic world, suggesting he was a Hellenistic Jew—a Jew who had adopted Greek culture and language.

Paul uses the Greek word 'syngenēs' (relative) for Andronicus. This can mean an actual blood relative but is also used more broadly to refer to a fellow countryman or fellow Israelite (cf. Rom 9:3). It is uncertain whether Paul means a close family relationship or simply that Andronicus was Jewish.

The fact that Andronicus came to faith 'before' Paul places his conversion very early, possibly in connection with the first Pentecost or the earliest missionary activity in Jerusalem after Jesus' resurrection (around AD 30–33).

Paul calls Andronicus his 'fellow prisoner' (Greek: synaichmalōtos), which literally means 'fellow captive'. The expression indicates that Andronicus had been imprisoned for the sake of faith. Paul was imprisoned on several occasions (cf. 2 Cor 11:23), and it is unknown when they shared imprisonment.

The debate over Junia/Junias has been central to discussions about women in apostolic ministry. The name in the accusative case (Iounian) can be interpreted as either the feminine form Junia or the masculine Junias. Recent scholarship and the earliest sources strongly support the feminine reading Junia, making the couple Andronicus and Junia an important witness to the role of women in the early church.

In Eastern church tradition, Andronicus is counted among the seventy disciples whom Jesus sent out (Luke 10:1). According to this tradition, he later became bishop in Pannonia (modern-day Hungary). These traditions cannot be confirmed historically but testify to the great respect for Andronicus in early Christianity.

The word 'apostle' (Greek: apostolos) is used in the New Testament in various senses—both of the twelve closest disciples of Jesus and more broadly of envoys or missionaries. That Andronicus is called prominent among the apostles likely suggests this broader usage, showing that the concept of apostle in the early church was more flexible than it often appears in later church tradition.
